section.title: Elihu's Third Speech
section.sectionRationale: Elihu's shortest speech targets a specific claim he attributes to Job, that righteousness profits a man nothing since God takes no notice of it either way. Elihu answers that human conduct, whether sin or righteousness, mainly affects other people, not God's own being, and that unanswered cries for help often stem from pride rather than genuine faith, since so few actually ask, 'Where is God my Maker, who gives songs in the night?'
section.thesis: Elihu is right that God's greatness is not increased or diminished by any human's righteousness or sin, but he is too quick to conclude that Job's unanswered cries must therefore be the empty pleas of a proud man rather than the honest lament of a genuine sufferer.
section.frameNote: Four movements: Elihu's charge that Job claims righteousness profits nothing; his argument that human conduct mainly affects fellow humans, not God directly; his claim that many cries under oppression go unanswered because no one truly seeks God as Maker; and his conclusion that Job speaks in vain, multiplying words without knowledge.

units.label: More righteous than God?
units.note: what profit is there in not sinning

verses.text: And Elihu went on to say:
“Do you think this is just? You say, ‘I am more righteous than God.’
For you ask, ‘What does it profit me, and what benefit do I gain apart from sin?’
I will reply to you and to your friends as well.

units.label: Your righteousness reaches man, not God
units.note: look to the heavens and see

verses.text: Look to the heavens and see; gaze at the clouds high above you.
If you sin, what do you accomplish against Him? If you multiply your transgressions, what do you do to Him?
If you are righteous, what do you give Him, or what does He receive from your hand?
Your wickedness affects only a man like yourself, and your righteousness only a son of {{adam|man}}.

units.label: Songs in the night
units.note: no one asks, Where is God my Maker

verses.text: Men cry out under great oppression; they plead for relief from the arm of the mighty.
But no one asks, ‘Where is God my Maker, who gives us {{zemirah|songs}} in the night,
who teaches us more than the beasts of the earth and makes us wiser than the birds of the air?’
There they cry out, but He does not answer, because of the pride of evil men.
Surely God does not listen to {{shav|empty}} pleas, and the Almighty does not take note of it.
How much less, then, when you say that you do not see Him, that your case is before Him and you must wait for Him,
and further, that in His anger He has not punished or taken much notice of folly!
So Job opens his mouth in vain and multiplies words without knowledge.”

adam.gloss: Son of man, humanity in general. Elihu insists both sin and righteousness land on fellow human beings, ben adam, rather than adding to or subtracting from God's own being, an argument meant to humble Job's implied claim that his suffering somehow proves God's unfairness toward him personally.

zemirah.gloss: Song, melody. Elihu's poignant question, 'where is God my Maker, who gives songs in the night,' pictures God as the source of comfort and even joy in the darkest hours, a gift Elihu says goes unsought by those who cry out only in pride rather than genuine faith.

shav.gloss: Emptiness, vanity, worthlessness. Elihu argues that God does not listen to shav, empty or hollow, pleas, cries that rise from wounded pride rather than humble trust, a claim he then applies, perhaps too quickly, to explain why Job feels unheard.

basic.context: Elihu answers a claim he attributes to Job, that there is no real benefit to righteousness since it does not seem to affect God's treatment of him one way or another. Elihu responds that human sin or righteousness mainly affects other humans, not God's own transcendent being, and that people often cry out to God from wounded pride rather than genuine faith, which is why, in Elihu's view, so many cries go unanswered.
basic.hermeneutics: Elihu's theological point about God's self sufficiency is sound and echoes Eliphaz's earlier argument in chapter 22; the risk, again, is applying a true general principle too confidently to Job's specific situation, effectively accusing Job of empty, prideful complaint rather than acknowledging that Job's confusion stems from a genuinely inexplicable providence.
basic.originalLanguages: Elihu insists that sin and righteousness reach only ben adam, one's fellow man, not God's own being. He pictures God as the one who gives zemirah, songs, in the night, a beautiful image of comfort largely unsought by people in their pride, and he concludes that shav, empty, pleas rightly go unanswered, a diagnosis he extends, not entirely fairly, to Job's own cries.
basic.typology: Elihu's picture of God as the giver of 'songs in the night' anticipates the fuller biblical pattern of God as comforter in darkness, ultimately embodied in Christ, who sang a hymn with His disciples on the night of His betrayal, Matthew 26:30, and who promises His presence in every dark hour.
basic.christ: Elihu asks whether anyone truly seeks 'God my Maker, who gives songs in the night'; Christ is the fullest answer to that question, the Maker who became flesh to dwell among sufferers, who sang a hymn on the very night He was betrayed, and who gives His people reason for songs even in their darkest nights, Acts 16:25, Psalm 42:8.
basic.god: God's greatness is not increased by human righteousness nor diminished by human sin, a point Scripture affirms elsewhere, Psalm 16:2, yet God is not indifferent to human cries; the whole book of Job, and especially its epilogue, shows a God who does hear, does answer, and does restore, even when the answer does not come on the timeline the sufferer expects.
basic.crossReferences: Psalm 16:2 affirms that human goodness adds nothing to God's own being. Psalm 42:8 speaks of God's song being with the psalmist in the night. Acts 16:25 pictures Paul and Silas singing hymns in prison at midnight. Matthew 26:30 has Jesus sing a hymn with His disciples before His arrest.
basic.oneStory: Elihu rightly says God's greatness does not depend on human conduct, but his charge that Job's cries are merely proud and empty misjudges a genuine sufferer. The Bible's fuller answer to Elihu's own beautiful question, who gives songs in the night, arrives in Christ, who not only gives songs in dark hours but entered the darkest night of all so that sufferers would never cry out to an truly absent God.

context.literary:
Job 35 is the shortest of Elihu's speeches, sixteen verses, and it is built as a rebuttal in three moves. In verses 1 to 4 Elihu names two things he says Job has claimed and promises to answer both Job and his friends. In verses 5 to 8 he sends Job's eyes up to the sky, and argues that neither sin nor righteousness can touch God. In verses 9 to 13 he turns to the oppressed who cry out and are not answered. Verses 14 to 16 apply the point to Job and close with the verdict that Job "opens his mouth in vain and multiplies words without knowledge."

The chapter is held together by a pair of opposites, up and down, far and near. The heavens and clouds are above, Job 35:5, and the man on earth is small. But the second half moves down among the oppressed and up again to God's ear. The sting is that the same distance which makes God untouchable also, on Elihu's account, makes Job's cry pointless.

Two lines break the pattern and give it beauty. Elihu quotes what no one asks in their distress: "Where is God my Maker, who gives us songs in the night, who teaches us more than the beasts of the earth and makes us wiser than the birds of the air?" Job 35:10-11. It is a quiet, generous sentence set in the middle of an argument otherwise sharp and cold.

The chapter also marks a shift in how Elihu handles Job's words. In chapter 33 he quoted Job closely. In chapter 34 he stretched. Here he reports questions that Job never asked in this form. Job 35:2 has him say "I am more righteous than God," which Job never says, and the mismatch is what the reader is meant to notice.
context.historical:
Elihu's counsel to look at the heavens fits the way the ancient world thought about God's remoteness. The sky was the standard sign of what is high and beyond reach. In Job 22:12 Eliphaz asks, "Is not God as high as the heavens?" and in the next verses imagines Job saying that thick clouds veil God so that He does not see. Elihu takes the same picture, though he draws a different conclusion. He is nearer to Eliphaz than he admits: his questions in Job 35:6-7 are close to Eliphaz's in Job 22:2-3, "Can a man be of use to God?... Does it delight the Almighty that you are righteous?"

The setting for the oppressed in Job 35:9 is a world where the powerful could take land, animals and labour with little check. Job himself has listed such wrongs in his own defence, in the chapters before. Elihu speaks about them in the abstract, and that is one more difference between him and Job, who had actually been seen among the poor and the widow.

"Songs in the night" belonged to Israel's practice of prayer. The Psalms speak of remembering God's song at night, Psalm 77:6, and of His song being with the psalmist, Psalm 42:8. Night was a time of fear and solitude, and turning it into praise was part of Israel's habit of prayer.

"Teaches us more than the beasts" turns a line of Job's own. In Job 12:7-8 Job told his friends to ask the animals and the birds, and they would instruct them. Elihu replies that God has given people more understanding than the animals have. The Old Testament sees human beings as made in the image of God, Genesis 1:27, and therefore able to ask the question that the beasts cannot: where is God my Maker?
context.canonical:
The idea that God needs nothing from us is deeply biblical. Psalm 16:2 says, "apart from You I have no good thing," and in Psalm 50:8-12 the LORD says He has no need of a bull from a stall, for the world and its fullness are His. Paul preaches on the Areopagus that God is not served by human hands, as if He needed anything, because He gives everyone life and breath, Acts 17:25. Elihu is standing on that ground in Job 35:6-7.

But Scripture does not let that truth stand alone. When David confesses, "Against You, You only, have I sinned," Psalm 51:4, he shows that sin is an offence against God as well as against people. Genesis 6:6 says the LORD was grieved in His heart over the sin of the earth, and Ephesians 4:30 warns believers not to grieve the Holy Spirit. Against Elihu's line in Job 35:8, that wickedness affects only "a man like yourself," these texts say that God is neither indifferent nor unmoved by sin.

The question about cries that are not answered runs through the Bible. Job 30:20 and Job 19:7 are cries of this kind. Psalm 22:2 says, "I cry out by day, O my God, but You do not answer." Psalm 22:24 says the LORD "has not despised or detested the torment of the afflicted... but has attended to his cry for help." Hebrews 5:7 says Jesus "was heard because of His reverence." The Bible contains cries that go unanswered for a time, and it insists that the answer comes.

Songs in the night are found from the exodus to the early church. Psalm 42:8 and Psalm 77:6 speak of them, and in Acts 16:25 Paul and Silas pray and sing hymns at midnight in prison.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The writer uses Elihu's third speech to show how a partial truth can turn into a wrong diagnosis. God's greatness is truly not enlarged by our goodness or reduced by our sin, and readers who forget it slip into thinking of religion as a way to put God in our debt. That is the mistake of the wicked in Job 21:15, who ask what they would gain by praying. Elihu wants Job to give up that view.

But the writer also lets the reader see that Job never held it. Job's complaint was never that righteousness earns nothing from God. His complaint is that he is treated as an enemy while innocent, and that his cries seem to go unheard, Job 30:20. To say that he claimed to be "more righteous than God" ignores Job's repeated wish to have his case heard before God, Job 13:3, and his willingness to say, "If I have sinned, what have I done to You?" Job 7:20.

The first hearers were meant to receive a real teaching, that God is self-sufficient and that God is the Maker who gives songs in the night, and to see it turned against a man who needed comfort. The chapter asks them to hold both: God is high and does not need us, and He is near enough to give songs. The writer has already shown the answer in the prologue, where the reader knows what Elihu does not, that Job's suffering is not about his profit from righteousness at all.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Elihu's speech describes what one man thinks. It does not tell us that unanswered cries are always proof of pride or that suffering people should stop complaining. The Bible itself gives sufferers words for complaint, the laments of Psalm 22 and Psalm 88, and there is no rebuke of them. Nothing in the book of Job commands us to silence a sufferer's questions, and the LORD's own answer in Job 38 is addressed to Job's cry.

What does apply is the invitation in the middle of the chapter: ask, in the dark, "Where is God my Maker, who gives us songs in the night?" That question is a good one for a person under pressure, and it points to the true source of comfort. It is also right to keep the doctrine of God's self-sufficiency, since it guards against thinking of faith as a bargain. What we may not do is use a true statement about God's greatness to tell someone that their pain is unimportant to Him. The Bible's usual pattern is to pair the two truths, as in Isaiah 57:15, where the high and holy One dwells with the contrite.

debates.question: Whose pride is in view in Job 35:12?

views.label: The pride of the oppressors
views.case: The verse says people cry out under oppression "because of the pride of evil men." On this reading the cries are unanswered because those who cause the suffering are proud, and Elihu says God does not act in the way the sufferers expect. The flow from verse 9 supports it, since the cry is the cry of the oppressed against the mighty.

views.label: The pride of the crying
views.case: The next verse says that God does not listen to empty pleas, which suggests the fault lies in those who cry. They cry as the beasts cry from pain, without asking where God their Maker is, Job 35:10. On this reading the cry itself is proud because it seeks relief and does not seek God.

debates.bearing: The Hebrew is compact and the BSB leaves the sense open. Either way, Elihu makes a claim about the heart behind the cry, and the book gives no support to the idea that every unanswered cry is a proud one. Job's cry was answered by the LORD, Job 38:1, and the Psalms show cries for help that God attends to, Psalm 22:24.

debates.question: Is Elihu's picture of a God untouched by human conduct right?

views.label: Yes, it defends God's freedom
views.case: Psalm 16:2, Psalm 50:8-12 and Acts 17:25 all say that God needs nothing. Elihu's argument rightly prevents anyone from imagining that righteousness puts God in our debt, or that sin can hurt Him in a way that threatens His being.

views.label: Only partly, because sin is against God
views.case: David says he has sinned against God only, Psalm 51:4, Genesis 6:6 says the LORD was grieved, and Ephesians 4:30 speaks of grieving the Holy Spirit. A picture in which our sin affects only other men leaves out the personal relationship at the heart of Scripture.

debates.bearing: Both are needed. God is not diminished by our sin, and He is truly wronged by it. Elihu's statement is safe as a statement about God's being and misleading as a statement about God's relationship with people.

study.originalLanguages:
Elihu's first charge in Job 35:2 turns on a small preposition. The BSB reads it as a comparison, "I am more righteous than God," but the same little word, min, carries other senses, and it is also behind the phrase in Job 32:2 that Job justified himself "rather than" God. Other English versions hear a claim to be right before God or to be cleared by Him. The variation is worth noticing because Job's real claim, in Job 13:18, was that he would be vindicated, and Job never asked to be superior to God. Reading Elihu with the mildest translation shows that even that reading is a stretch from anything Job said.

In Job 35:3 the question "What does it profit me?" uses the verb for being of use. It is the same idea that the wicked voice in Job 21:15, "what would we gain if we pray to Him?", and that Eliphaz raised in Job 22:2 with the question, "Can a man be of use to God?" Job answered the wicked's line by saying he stayed far from their counsel, Job 21:16. So three earlier voices already hold the idea Elihu uses here, and the passage is a small anthology of the book's arguments about usefulness.

The two verbs in Job 35:6-7 are worth setting side by side. The first asks what you can "accomplish" against God if you sin, and the second what you can "give" Him if you are righteous. Both are the language of transactions. Job had asked a kindred question in Job 7:20, "If I have sinned, what have I done to You, O watcher of mankind?" Elihu takes that question and answers it more bluntly than Job expected: nothing at all.

The balance of Job 35:8 is worth noticing. Wickedness reaches "a man like yourself" and righteousness "a son of man," in Hebrew ben adam, the ordinary phrase for a human being. It is the phrase used in Psalm 8:4, where the psalmist wonders what a "son of man" is that God should care for him. Elihu uses the term to stress human smallness, and the Psalm uses it to marvel at God's care.

In Job 35:10 the word for "God" is Eloah, a form most at home in the book of Job, and it is joined to the word for "my Maker." Elihu has spoken of God as his Maker before, in Job 32:22, and will again in Job 36:3. The word for "songs" is zemirot, the word from which Israel's psalm-singing is named, and it appears in the phrase "songs in the night." Psalm 42:8 and Psalm 77:6 speak of a song at night in different words.

The word for "empty" in Job 35:13 means what is vain or worthless. It has a sound of hollowness, and Elihu applies it to pleas that come without seeking God. In Job 35:16 he applies the same idea to Job, saying he opens his mouth "in vain" and multiplies words without knowledge. The claim is a sharp one. Yet the phrase "words without knowledge" comes back in Job 38:2 and Job 42:3. The LORD's own use of it is a reminder that Elihu is not the only one who charges Job with speaking without knowledge, and that Job agrees in the end.

Verse 15 is textually difficult, and English versions differ noticeably in it. The BSB understands Elihu to say that Job complains that God has not punished or taken much notice of folly. Readers should not put weight on any single word in the verse.

typology.type: God who gives songs in the night, Job 35:10
typology.fulfillment: Elihu names the Maker who gives songs in the dark. The Old Testament repeats it in Psalm 42:8 and Psalm 77:6, and Acts 16:25 shows it in the life of the church, where Paul and Silas sing in a prison at midnight. Jesus fulfils the picture: on the night He was betrayed, He and His disciples sang a hymn before going out to the Mount of Olives, Matthew 26:30, and then He entered Gethsemane. The correspondence is that the song is sung in the very darkness it is meant for. The type falls short because Elihu's songs are an occasion for comfort, while Jesus' song led to the cross, where the darkness was borne for others.

typology.type: The cry that seems unanswered, Job 35:12-13
typology.fulfillment: Elihu says there are cries God does not answer. The Old Testament expresses that felt silence, as in Psalm 22:1-2, and Jesus took the psalm's first words on the cross, "My God, my God, why have You forsaken me?" Matthew 27:46. The cry looked like one that God did not hear. Yet the psalm ends with the promise that He "has not hidden His face from him, but has attended to his cry for help," Psalm 22:24, and Hebrews 5:7 says Jesus "was heard because of His reverence." The type is turned over: the apparently unanswered cry is answered in the resurrection. It differs from Job in that Jesus' cry was not the cry of pride but of obedience.

typology.type: Righteousness that reaches a son of man, Job 35:8
typology.fulfillment: Elihu says a man's righteousness affects only a son of man. In Christ the phrase becomes the promise. Jesus calls Himself the Son of Man, and His obedience brings righteousness to many: "through the obedience of the one man the many will be made righteous," Romans 5:19. What Elihu meant to shrink, the reach of one human's righteousness, is enlarged beyond measure, though it is the righteousness of one who is also God. The type does not fit neatly, since Elihu meant his line as a limit. It works as an echo, showing how an Old Testament phrase is filled by the gospel.

study.christ:
The chapter leads to Christ most directly through its best line: "Where is God my Maker, who gives us songs in the night?" Job 35:10. The Old Testament answers by pointing to the psalmist's song at night, but the gospel names the Maker who came near. John says all things were made through the Word, and the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, John 1:3 and 1:14. The Maker Elihu wants people to ask for is the one who took a body, a night and a garden.

On the night of His betrayal, Jesus and His disciples sang a hymn and went out to the Mount of Olives, Matthew 26:30. Then in Gethsemane His anguish was such that He prayed more earnestly and His sweat became like drops of blood, Luke 22:41-44. That is the song in the night at its deepest, a song sung by One who was about to enter a night with no comfort. Acts 16:25 shows the fruit of it in the church, where prisoners hear Paul and Silas sing at midnight.

The chapter also leads to Christ by contrast with its claim that some cries go unanswered. Elihu says God does not listen to empty pleas, Job 35:13. Jesus cried out with the words of Psalm 22:1, and Hebrews 5:7 says that with loud cries and tears He "was heard because of His reverence." The cry that seemed to go unheard in the darkness of the cross was answered on the third day, and it answers Job's cry too. God has "attended to his cry for help," Psalm 22:24.

A third connection is the question of what our righteousness can do. Elihu says it gives God nothing, Job 35:7. That is right in one sense, and the gospel does not deny it. Jesus' righteousness was not given to God as a gift He lacked, but to us as a gift we lacked: God made Him who knew no sin to be sin for us, that we might become the righteousness of God in Him, 2 Corinthians 5:21. In Romans 5:19 the obedience of the one man makes the many righteous. Elihu's line about a "son of man" thus finds an unexpected fulfilment in the Son of Man.

A caution keeps the reading honest. Elihu does not speak of Jesus, and the chapter's charge against Job is unfair. It would be wrong to say that Elihu's line about songs is a prediction. The connection rests on the New Testament's own picture of Jesus singing on the night of His arrest and on its use of Psalm 22 for His cry.
study.god:
The God of this chapter is the God who is high above us and who needs nothing. "Look to the heavens and see; gaze at the clouds high above you," Job 35:5. Elihu asks Job to consider that distance and to see that a creature's conduct cannot enlarge or diminish the Creator. That is what theologians call God's self-sufficiency, and it is taught in Psalm 50:8-12 and Acts 17:25. It is a doctrine that keeps worship free of bargaining. We do not obey in order to keep God in business.

It is a doctrine that also has a sharp edge. If it is left alone, it makes God sound like a distant power and turns our prayers into noise. Elihu comes close to that. The book's fuller picture keeps the height and adds the nearness. Isaiah 57:15 says the high and lofty One who inhabits eternity also dwells with the contrite, and Psalm 113:5-6 says He is enthroned on high and yet stoops to look on the heavens and the earth.

God is the Maker who teaches. "He teaches us more than the beasts of the earth and makes us wiser than the birds of the air," Job 35:11. This assigns dignity to human beings. We are capable of asking about God, and we are given the understanding to do so. The claim is consistent with the creation of man in God's image, Genesis 1:27, and with the breath of God that Elihu spoke of earlier, Job 32:8.

God is the one who gives songs in the night. It is a gift, not a reward. The song comes from Him, and Psalm 42:8 says that at night His song is with me as a prayer to the God of my life. This tells us that comfort in the dark is a work of God, not a mood we generate.

There is a tension between what Elihu says and what the LORD does. Elihu says God does not take note of empty pleas, Job 35:13, and that Job speaks without knowledge. Yet the LORD in Job 38:1 answers Job out of the whirlwind. Job's cry, which Elihu calls vain, is the one God chooses to answer. It teaches that God's hearing does not depend on the sufferer having the right theology. And the book of Job ends with the LORD saying Job spoke of Him rightly, Job 42:7. The chapter teaches worship to set the great distance next to the great nearness, so that we bow before the Almighty and ask, in the dark, where our Maker is.

crossReferences.note: Eliphaz asks whether a man can be of use to God, and whether it delights the Almighty that you are righteous. Elihu's questions in Job 35:6-7 are close to these. The parallel shows that Elihu is not saying anything new here, and that the friends' arguments were already circling the same idea.

Job asks, "If I have sinned, what have I done to You, O watcher of mankind?" Elihu's line in Job 35:6 is an answer to that question, though Job was not making a claim about his righteousness but crying out in distress. The link shows how Elihu reads Job's pain as a doctrine.

The wicked ask what they would gain if they prayed, and Job says he stays far from their counsel. The words Elihu puts in Job's mouth in Job 35:3 are closer to the wicked's than to Job's, which means Elihu is blaming Job for what he explicitly refused.

Job tells his friends to ask the animals and the birds, and they will teach. Elihu says in Job 35:11 that God teaches us more than the beasts. He answers Job's own image and reminds readers that human beings are made to seek the Maker.

Job says he cries to God for help and God does not answer. This is the complaint Elihu addresses in Job 35:12-14. Placing the two together shows that Job's cry is real anguish, and that Elihu labels it pride.

"Apart from You I have no good thing." The psalm states the truth behind Job 35:7, that God receives nothing from us that He lacked. It also shows that this truth was prayed as a joy by a worshipper, not used as a stick against a sufferer.

By day the LORD decrees His loving devotion, and at night His song is with the psalmist as a prayer. This is the fullest Old Testament echo of Job 35:10. It also gives the reason a person can sing in the dark, which is that the loving devotion of God has been decreed for the day.

The LORD has not despised or detested the torment of the afflicted and has attended to his cry for help. The verse answers Elihu's claim in Job 35:12-13 that some cries go unanswered, and it is the psalm Jesus prayed from the cross.

David says he has sinned against God only. The verse qualifies Job 35:8, since it shows that a person's sin is an offence against God, not only against other people. God is not harmed by it, and He is truly wronged by it.

Paul preaches that God is not served by human hands as if He needed anything, because He gives everyone life and breath. It is the New Testament statement of Elihu's point in Job 35:6-7, joined to the truth that God is the giver of all.

Jesus and His disciples sing a hymn before going out to the Mount of Olives on the night of His betrayal. It is the clearest gospel picture of a song in the night, and it shows the Maker of Job 35:10 among those who sing.

Jesus offered prayers and petitions with loud cries and tears and was heard because of His reverence. It answers the worry of Job 35:12-13 about unanswered cries, and shows that a cry offered in obedient trust is never empty.

study.oneStory:
At the start of the Bible, God makes human beings in His image and breathes into them, and they are set in a garden to know Him. Job 35 asks what has become of that knowing. People cry out under oppression, but "no one asks, 'Where is God my Maker?'" Job 35:10. That is the fall in a sentence. We feel pain, and we do not seek the Giver. Elihu is describing the ruin of Genesis 3 in the language of a wisdom speech.

The chapter also sets up the Bible's long argument about distance and nearness. God is above the heavens and needs nothing. Yet He walked in the garden, Genesis 3:8, spoke to Abraham as a friend, met Israel on the mountain and set His name in the tabernacle. The Old Testament keeps both truths together, and the Psalms teach sufferers to bring their cries to the God who is high. Job's cry, which Elihu calls vain, is one of the great cries of that tradition.

Job's friends have been arguing that righteousness pays, and Elihu now says it gives God nothing. Between the two lies the question of what a relationship with God really is. Not a wage, and not a gift from us to God. It is the fellowship of a Maker with His creatures, in which the giving is on God's side. The prophets and the Psalms fill this in, and the gospel completes it. "Songs in the night" become the church's practice, Acts 16:25.

In Christ the two distances are bridged. The Maker becomes flesh, John 1:14. He sings, He cries out, He is heard, and His righteousness is given to many, Romans 5:19. The cry that seemed to go unheard is answered in the resurrection, Hebrews 5:7.

In the new creation, the night is gone. "There will be no more night in the city," Revelation 22:5, and the people of God will see His face, Revelation 22:4. The question "Where is God my Maker?" is answered by sight. The songs that began in the dark, in prison cells and sickrooms, become the song of the redeemed.

sermon.title: Job: Rebuked in Suffering
sermon.why: Piper's sermon on Job 32:1-37:24 treats Elihu's speeches as a unified rebuke and preparation for God's own answer, engaging directly with this speech's argument that God's justice and self sufficiency mean Job's complaints rest on a misunderstanding rather than genuine grievance.

quiz.q: What claim does Elihu attribute to Job at the start of chapter 35?

options.text: That righteousness profits a man nothing, since sin or virtue seems to make no difference to how God treats him.
options.note: Verses 2-3 frame this as the specific complaint Elihu is answering.

options.text: That Job wants to abandon belief in God entirely.
options.note: Job's complaint concerns the apparent lack of visible reward for righteousness, not abandoning belief in God.

options.text: That Job believes his friends are entirely right about him.
options.note: Job has consistently opposed his friends' theology, not agreed with it.

options.text: That Job believes there is little practical difference between the righteous and the wicked in how life actually turns out.
options.note: Close, this captures much of Job's real complaint about the prospering wicked in chapter 21, but Elihu's paraphrase here makes the stronger claim that righteousness itself profits nothing at all.

quiz.q: What is Elihu's main argument in 35:5-8?

options.text: Human sin or righteousness mainly affects other people, not God's own transcendent being.
options.note: Verses 6-8 state this directly, that neither adds to nor takes from what God is in Himself.

options.text: God is completely indifferent to human behavior.
options.note: Elihu's point is about God's self sufficiency, not indifference; the rest of the book shows God deeply engaged with human conduct.

options.text: God is pleased or displeased by human conduct much the way one person is affected by another.
options.note: Close, but Elihu's specific point is the opposite: God's own being is not increased or diminished by human conduct the way a fellow human's would be.

options.text: Human behavior directly changes God's essential nature.
options.note: Elihu argues precisely the opposite, that God's own being is unaffected either way.

quiz.q: According to Elihu, why do many cries under oppression go unanswered, 35:9-13?

options.text: Because people cry out from pride rather than genuine trust, seeking relief without truly seeking God as Maker.
options.note: Verse 12 explicitly attributes unanswered cries to 'the pride of evil men.'

options.text: Because God is powerless to help the oppressed.
options.note: Elihu's whole speech assumes God's active power and sovereignty; powerlessness is not his claim.

options.text: Because oppression does not actually exist in the world.
options.note: Verse 9 explicitly acknowledges real oppression and real cries for help.

options.text: Because people often ask for relief from circumstances without truly seeking a relationship with God as their Maker.
options.note: Very close to Elihu's actual point in verses 10-12, though it softens his sharper diagnosis that the specific obstacle is human pride.

quiz.q: How does Elihu's question, 'where is God my Maker, who gives songs in the night,' 35:10, ultimately get answered in the Bible's larger story?

options.text: In Christ, who entered the darkest night of betrayal singing a hymn, and who gives His people songs of hope in their own darkness.
options.note: Matthew 26:30 and Acts 16:25 both show this pattern of God's presence and song even amid suffering.

options.text: The Bible mainly answers this through the Psalms, without a fuller answer given in the person of Christ.
options.note: Close, Psalm 42:8 does pick up this theme, but the New Testament's fullest answer comes specifically through Christ, who embodies God's presence and song in the darkest night of all.

options.text: By teaching that God never gives comfort during suffering.
options.note: The pattern across Scripture is the opposite, God's comforting presence precisely in dark seasons.

options.text: By proving that no one can ever know God as Maker.
options.note: Elihu's question is rhetorical, lamenting that few seek this knowledge, not declaring it impossible.

quiz.q: How should Elihu's true premise about God's self sufficiency be weighed against his specific charge against Job?

options.text: The premise about God's transcendence is sound, but applying it to conclude Job's cries are empty and prideful goes beyond what the book itself confirms.
options.note: God's epilogue verdict, 42:7-8, favors Job's honesty over the confident, harsh diagnoses of both the friends and, in places, Elihu.

options.text: The premise is sound, and Job likely does need some humbling, even if not exactly in the way Elihu describes.
options.note: Close to a fair balanced reading, since Job is indeed humbled in chapters 38-42, though the book's own verdict in 42:7-8 still favors Job's honest speech over the friends' and, implicitly, over Elihu's harsher charge.

options.text: Neither the premise nor the charge has any value.
options.note: The premise about God's self sufficiency is sound theology, affirmed elsewhere in Scripture, even if the specific application to Job overreaches.

options.text: The premise is false, but the charge against Job is entirely correct.
options.note: The premise about divine self sufficiency is true; it is the specific application to Job that appears overreaching.

questions: Elihu argues that our righteousness or sin mainly affects other people, not God's own being. How does remembering this shape the way you think about the purpose of living righteously?
Elihu asks why so few seek 'God my Maker, who gives songs in the night.' Have you experienced God giving you an unexpected song, comfort, or hope in a genuinely dark season?
Elihu diagnosed Job's cries as empty pride, but God later vindicated Job's honesty. How can you tell the difference between prideful complaint and honest lament in your own prayers?
Christ sang a hymn with His disciples the very night He was betrayed. What would it look like for you to choose worship or gratitude in the middle of your own hardest night?

Elihu's true theology was applied to Job too quickly and too harshly. When you want to offer someone spiritual truth in their suffering, how can you first make sure you have truly listened to their actual pain?

translationNotes.note: 'What benefit do I gain apart from sin' is Elihu's paraphrase of Job's implied complaint; the exact phrase does not appear verbatim earlier in Job's speeches, suggesting Elihu may be summarizing rather than quoting directly.
'Songs in the night' likely refers to songs of praise or comfort given even amid affliction, a phrase with resonance in Psalm 42:8 and later Christian hymnody about finding joy in suffering.
'Empty pleas' translates shav, which can also mean vanity or falsehood; Elihu's point is that hollow, self focused cries, rather than all prayer, fail to receive a hearing.
